notes.front: What is a blob container?
notes.back: A grouping of blobs inside a storage account, similar to a directory in a file system.
notes.explanation: An account can hold an unlimited number of containers, and each container an unlimited number of blobs.
notes.example: Like a top-level folder on a shared drive that can hold any number of files.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Containers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A container organizes a set of blobs, similar to a directory in a file system. A storage account can include an unlimited number of containers, and a container can store an unlimited number of blobs.

notes.front: What is rehydration of a blob?
notes.back: Moving an archived blob back to an online tier (hot, cool or cold) so that it can be read.
notes.explanation: Rehydration can take up to 15 hours, depending on the priority you choose for it.
notes.example: Like ordering a box back from an off-site records store before you can open it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Archive access tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To read or download a blob in the archive tier, you must first rehydrate it to an online tier, either hot, cool, or cold. Data in the archive tier can take up to 15 hours to rehydrate, depending on the priority you specify for the rehydration operation.

notes.front: What does blob soft delete do?
notes.back: It keeps deleted or overwritten blobs, snapshots and versions for a set period so they can be restored.
notes.explanation: During the retention period an object can be restored to its state when deleted; afterwards it is permanently deleted.
notes.example: Like a recycle bin for single files that empties itself after a set number of days.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Blob soft delete protects an individual blob, snapshot, or version from accidental deletes or overwrites by keeping the deleted data in the system for a specified period. During the retention period, you can restore a soft-deleted object to its state at the time it was deleted. After the retention period expires, the object is permanently deleted.

notes.front: What does container soft delete do?
notes.back: It keeps deleted containers in the account for a set period so they can be restored with their contents.
notes.explanation: A restored container returns with its contents as they were when it was deleted.
notes.example: Like a recycle bin that catches whole folders rather than single files.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for containers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Container soft delete protects your containers from being accidentally deleted by maintaining the deleted containers in the storage account for a specified period of time. During the retention period, you can restore a soft-deleted container and its contents to the container's state at the time it was deleted.

notes.front: What is a share snapshot in Azure Files?
notes.back: A point-in-time, read-only copy of an Azure file share’s data.
notes.explanation: Snapshots are taken for the whole share, but you can retrieve individual files from them.
notes.example: Like a dated photocopy of a whole filing cabinet from which you can pull single pages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Share snapshot capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A share snapshot is a point-in-time, read-only copy of your data. Share snapshot capability is provided at the file share level. Retrieval is provided at the individual file level, to allow for restoring individual files.

notes.front: What is soft delete for file shares?
notes.back: A setting that keeps deleted file shares for a retention period so a mistakenly deleted share can be recovered.
notes.explanation: Deleted shares are kept in a soft-deleted state until the retention period ends, then permanently deleted.
notes.example: Like a recycle bin for whole network drives.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Files offers soft delete, which allows you to recover your file share if you mistakenly deleted it. ## How soft delete works When you enable soft delete, the system retains deleted file shares in a soft deleted state for the defined retention period before permanently deleting them.

notes.front: What is a blob lifecycle management policy?
notes.back: A rule-based policy that automatically moves blobs to cooler tiers or deletes them when they are no longer needed.
notes.explanation: Its aim is to optimise storage costs as data ages.
notes.example: Like a records schedule that sends old files to the basement and later shreds them, without anyone lifting a box.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By using blob lifecycle management, customers can proactively optimize costs by implementing rule-based policies that automatically transition data to cooler tiers or expire it when it's no longer needed.

notes.front: What is blob versioning?
notes.back: A storage account setting that automatically keeps previous versions of blobs.
notes.explanation: Earlier versions let you recover data after a blob is modified or deleted.
notes.example: Like a document editor’s version history, saved on every change.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can enable Blob storage versioning to automatically maintain previous versions of an object. When you enable blob versioning, you can access earlier versions of a blob to recover your data if it's modified or deleted.

notes.front: Can one Azure file share serve both Server Message Block and Network File System clients?
notes.back: No. Each share uses one protocol, although one storage account can hold shares of both kinds.
notes.explanation: The protocol is chosen per share, not per storage account.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Plan an Azure Files deployment”, “Available protocols” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure file shares don't support both the SMB and NFS protocols on the same file share, although you can create SMB and NFS Azure file shares within the same storage account.

notes.front: Which client operating systems suit Network File System shares, compared with Server Message Block shares?
notes.back: Network File System: Linux only. Server Message Block: Windows, Linux and macOS.
notes.explanation: The protocol is one of the key decisions when planning an Azure Files deployment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Plan an Azure Files deployment” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Which protocol? SMB (Windows/Linux/macOS) or NFS (Linux only)?

notes.front: Which media tiers can Server Message Block shares use, compared with Network File System shares?
notes.back: Server Message Block: solid-state or hard disk. Network File System: solid-state only.
notes.explanation: So a Network File System share never runs on the hard disk media tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Plan an Azure Files deployment”, “Available protocols” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Available media tiers | SSD and HDD | SSD only

notes.front: A Linux-only analytics cluster needs hard links and symbolic links on its shared file storage. Which Azure Files protocol fits?
notes.back: Network File System.
notes.choices:
A) Server Message Block
B) Network File System
C) Either: both support hard links
D) Neither: Azure Files has no link support
notes.choicesExplained: A doesn’t support hard or symbolic links. C and D are wrong because support differs by protocol: only Network File System shares have it.
notes.explanation: Hard and symbolic links are supported on Network File System shares and not on Server Message Block shares.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Plan an Azure Files deployment”, “Available protocols” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Hard link support | Not supported | Supported | | Symbolic link support | Not supported | Supported |

notes.front: How do classic file shares differ from file shares created with the Microsoft.FileShares resource provider?
notes.back: Classic shares live inside a storage account; Microsoft.FileShares shares are top-level resources with no storage account.
notes.explanation: The top-level model simplifies management with per-share networking, billing and security, but is currently for Network File System shares only.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Plan an Azure Files deployment”, “Management concepts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deploy file shares within a storage account. Supports SMB and NFS, SSD and HDD, all redundancy types, and all regions. - **File shares (Microsoft.FileShares resource provider)**: Deploy file shares as top-level Azure resources without a storage account. Simplify management with per-share networking, billing, and security. Currently only available for NFS file shares.

notes.front: Which Azure Files billing model does Microsoft recommend for all new file share deployments?
notes.back: Provisioned v2.
notes.explanation: Provisioned v1 and pay-as-you-go remain fully supported for new and existing deployments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a storage account for classic file shares” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We recommend using the provisioned v2 billing model for all new file share deployments. The provisioned v1 and pay-as-you-go billing models remain fully supported for new and existing deployments.

notes.front: Which Azure Files billing model offers only solid-state shares, with no hard disk option?
notes.back: Provisioned v1.
notes.explanation: Provisioned v2 offers both solid-state and hard disk shares and pay-as-you-go only hard disk, so provisioned v1 is the solid-state-only model; its accounts use the `FileStorage` kind.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a provisioned v1 or pay-as-you-go storage account (PowerShell)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create a provisioned v1 storage account (SSD), set `storageAccountKind` to FileStorage. To create a pay-as-you-go storage account (HDD), set `storageAccountKind` to StorageV2.

notes.front: Which Azure Files billing model is for hard disk shares only and needs a general-purpose v2 (`StorageV2`) account?
notes.back: Pay-as-you-go.
notes.explanation: Provisioned file shares, by contrast, need the `FileStorage` account kind.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Provisioned file shares require a *FileStorage* storage account kind, and pay-as-you-go file shares (HDD only) require a *StorageV2 (general purpose v2)* storage account kind.

notes.front: On a provisioned file share, are you billed for the storage you provision or the storage you use?
notes.back: The storage you provision, regardless of actual usage.
notes.explanation: The provisioned amount is what determines that part of the bill.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a provisioned v2 classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The actual provisioned storage capacity is the amount that you're billed for regardless of actual usage.

notes.front: You are planning a brand-new Azure file share deployment and want to follow Microsoft’s recommendation. Which billing model do you pick?
notes.back: Provisioned v2.
notes.choices:
A) Provisioned v2
B) Provisioned v1
C) Pay-as-you-go
D) Any: Microsoft recommends none over the others
notes.choicesExplained: B and C remain fully supported but are not the recommended choice for new deployments. D is wrong because a recommendation exists.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends provisioned v2 for all new file share deployments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a storage account for classic file shares” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We recommend using the provisioned v2 billing model for all new file share deployments.

notes.front: Which redundancy options are available for solid-state (premium) Azure file shares?
notes.back: LRS and ZRS only.
notes.explanation: All four options, including GRS and GZRS, are offered for hard disk Server Message Block shares.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Files offers locally redundant storage (LRS), zone-redundant storage (ZRS), geo-redundant storage (GRS), and geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) options for HDD SMB file shares. SSD file shares are only available for the LRS and ZRS redundancy types.

notes.front: A team wants a solid-state file share whose data is also copied to a secondary region. Can one share meet both needs?
notes.back: No. Solid-state shares support only LRS or ZRS; geo-redundancy needs a hard disk share.
notes.explanation: GRS and GZRS are offered only for hard disk Server Message Block shares.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Files offers locally redundant storage (LRS), zone-redundant storage (ZRS), geo-redundant storage (GRS), and geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) options for HDD SMB file shares. SSD file shares are only available for the LRS and ZRS redundancy types.

notes.front: How do the two media tiers for classic file shares differ?
notes.back: Solid-state (premium): single-digit millisecond latency. Hard disk (standard): cost-effective general-purpose storage.
notes.explanation: The choice trades lower latency against lower cost.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure classic file shares offer two media tiers: SSD (premium), with single-digit millisecond latency, and HDD (standard), for cost-effective general purpose storage.

notes.front: A latency-sensitive app needs a file share that answers in single-digit milliseconds. Which media tier fits?
notes.back: Solid-state (premium).
notes.choices:
A) Hard disk (standard)
B) Solid-state (premium)
C) The archive access tier
D) The cool access tier
notes.choicesExplained: A is the cost-effective general-purpose tier, not the low-latency one. C and D are blob access tiers, not file share media tiers.
notes.explanation: Only the solid-state tier offers single-digit millisecond latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure classic file shares offer two media tiers: SSD (premium), with single-digit millisecond latency, and HDD (standard), for cost-effective general purpose storage.

notes.front: Where in the portal do you start creating a classic file share in an existing storage account?
notes.back: In the account’s Data storage menu, select Classic file shares, then + File share.
notes.explanation: The listing first shows any existing shares, or an empty table if there are none.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a provisioned v2 classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Go to your storage account. From the service menu, under **Data storage**, select **Classic file shares**. 2. In the file share listing, you should see any previously created file shares in this storage account or an empty table if no file shares exist. Select **+ File share** to create a new file share.

notes.front: Which characters may an Azure file share name contain?
notes.back: Lowercase letters, numbers and single hyphens; it must start and end with a lowercase letter or number.
notes.explanation: Two hyphens in a row are not allowed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a provisioned v2 classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The name of your file share must be all lowercase letters, numbers, and single hyphens, and must begin and end with a lowercase letter or number. The name can't contain two consecutive hyphens.

notes.front: Which protocol does a new classic file share use unless you choose otherwise?
notes.back: Server Message Block; selecting Network File System creates a version 4.1 share.
notes.explanation: The protocol is set on the new share’s Basics tab.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create a provisioned v2 classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Protocol:** The file sharing protocol to use on the share. By default, new shares use the SMB protocol. Select the NFS protocol to create an NFSv4.1 share.

notes.front: You are about to migrate a large number of files into a new pay-as-you-go file share. Which access tier should the share use first?
notes.back: Transaction optimised, then switch to a lower tier after the migration if needed.
notes.explanation: That tier minimises transaction expenses while the migration runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Create an Azure classic file share”, “Create an HDD pay-as-you-go classic file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pick the _transaction optimized_ access tier during a migration to minimize transaction expenses, and then switch to a lower tier if needed after the migration is complete.

notes.front: How long may a container name be, and which characters may it use?
notes.back: 3 to 63 characters: lowercase letters, numbers and dashes, starting with a letter or number.
notes.explanation: Two or more dashes in a row are not permitted.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Containers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Container names can be between 3 and 63 characters long. - Container names must start with a letter or number, and can contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and the dash (-) character. - Two or more consecutive dash characters aren't permitted in container names.

notes.front: Which of these is a valid blob container name?
notes.back: site-images-01
notes.choices:
A) Site-Images
B) site--images
C) site-images-01
D) -siteimages
notes.choicesExplained: A has capital letters. B has two consecutive dashes. D starts with a dash instead of a letter or number.
notes.explanation: It uses only lowercase letters, numbers and single dashes, starts with a letter and is 3 to 63 characters long.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Containers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Container names can be between 3 and 63 characters long. - Container names must start with a letter or number, and can contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and the dash (-) character. - Two or more consecutive dash characters aren't permitted in container names.

notes.front: Which blob type stores text and binary data in blocks that can be managed individually, up to about 190.7 TiB?
notes.back: Block blob.
notes.explanation: Each block of data can be managed on its own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Block blobs** store text and binary data. Block blobs are made up of blocks of data that can be managed individually. Block blobs can store up to about 190.7 TiB.

notes.front: Which blob type is optimised for append operations, such as logging data from virtual machines?
notes.back: Append blob.
notes.explanation: It is built from blocks like a block blob, but tuned for adding data to the end.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Append blobs** are made up of blocks like block blobs, but they're optimized for append operations. Append blobs are ideal for scenarios such as logging data from virtual machines.

notes.front: Which blob type stores random-access files up to 8 TiB and serves as disks for Azure virtual machines?
notes.back: Page blob.
notes.explanation: Page blobs hold the virtual hard drive files that act as those disks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Blob Storage”, “Blobs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Page blobs** store random access files up to 8 TiB in size. Page blobs store virtual hard drive (VHD) files and serve as disks for Azure virtual machines.

notes.front: A website stores its product photos and demo videos in Blob Storage. Which blob type should they be?
notes.back: Block blobs.
notes.choices:
A) Block blobs
B) Append blobs
C) Page blobs
D) Any type: the choice makes no difference
notes.choicesExplained: B is optimised for appending, as in logging. C is for random-access files such as virtual machine disks. D is wrong because each type suits different data.
notes.explanation: Block blobs are ideal for text and binary data such as files, images and videos, and most Blob Storage scenarios use them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Upload, download, and list blobs with the Azure portal”, “Upload a block blob” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Block blobs consist of blocks of data assembled to make a blob. Most scenarios that use Blob storage employ block blobs. Block blobs are ideal for storing text and binary data in the cloud, like files, images, and videos.

notes.front: You create a container in the portal for public web images and accept every default. Anonymous visitors can’t load the images. Why?
notes.back: The default anonymous access level for a new container is Private (no anonymous access).
notes.explanation: The anonymous access level is set per container while creating it, and the default allows no anonymous reads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Upload, download, and list blobs with the Azure portal”, “Create a container” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Set the level of anonymous access to the container. The default level is **Private (no anonymous access)**.

notes.front: Where in the portal do you create a new blob container?
notes.back: In the storage account’s Data storage section, select Containers, then + Container.
notes.explanation: Containers are listed under the account’s Data storage section.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Quickstart: Upload, download, and list blobs with the Azure portal”, “Create a container” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the left menu for the storage account, scroll to the **Data storage** section, then select **Containers**. 1. Select the **+ Container** button.

notes.front: Data in the cool tier should be stored for a minimum of {{c1::30}} days.
notes.explanation: Cool has lower storage costs but higher access costs than hot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data in the cool tier should be stored for a minimum of **30** days. The cool tier has lower storage costs and higher access costs compared to the hot tier.

notes.front: Data in the cold tier should be stored for a minimum of {{c1::90}} days.
notes.explanation: Cold is for rarely accessed data that still needs fast retrieval, and it costs less to store than cool.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An online tier optimized for storing data that is rarely accessed or modified, but still requires fast retrieval. Data in the cold tier should be stored for a minimum of **90** days. The cold tier has lower storage costs and higher access costs compared to the cool tier.

notes.front: Data in the archive tier should be stored for a minimum of {{c1::180}} days.
notes.explanation: Archive is an offline tier with latency on the order of hours, for rarely accessed data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An offline tier optimized for storing data that is rarely accessed, and that has flexible latency requirements, on the order of hours. Data in the archive tier should be stored for a minimum of **180** days.

notes.front: Weekly exports are read now and then, must open instantly, and are deleted after about 45 days. Which tier costs least without early deletion charges?
notes.back: Cool.
notes.choices:
A) Hot
B) Cool
C) Cold
D) Archive
notes.choicesExplained: A has the highest storage costs. C expects 90 days and D expects 180, so deleting at 45 days brings early deletion charges; D is also offline.
notes.explanation: Cool expects at least 30 days, which 45 days meets, and it stores more cheaply than hot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data in the cool tier should be stored for a minimum of **30** days. The cool tier has lower storage costs and higher access costs compared to the hot tier.

notes.front: Scanned forms are kept for two years, are rarely opened, but must open in milliseconds when needed. Which tier fits best?
notes.back: Cold.
notes.choices:
A) Hot
B) Cool
C) Cold
D) Archive
notes.choicesExplained: A and B cost more to store for rarely used data. D is offline, with retrieval measured in hours.
notes.explanation: Cold is the online tier for rarely accessed data that still needs fast retrieval, with lower storage costs than cool.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An online tier optimized for storing data that is rarely accessed or modified, but still requires fast retrieval. Data in the cold tier should be stored for a minimum of **90** days. The cold tier has lower storage costs and higher access costs compared to the cool tier.

notes.front: A blob is moved to the archive tier and deleted 60 days later. What extra charge applies?
notes.back: An early deletion fee equal to 120 more days of archive storage (180 minus 60).
notes.explanation: The fee covers the days still left of the 180-day minimum.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Archive access tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For example, if a blob is moved to the archive tier and then deleted or moved to the hot tier after 45 days, you'll be charged an early deletion fee equivalent to 135 (180 minus 45) days of storing that blob in the archive tier.

notes.front: What can you still read for a blob that is in the archive tier?
notes.back: Its metadata: you can list the blob and its properties, metadata and index tags.
notes.explanation: Metadata is read-only there, but index tags can still be written.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Archive access tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An archived blob's metadata remains available for read access, so that you can list the blob and its properties, metadata, and index tags. Metadata for a blob in the archive tier is read-only, while blob index tags can be read or written.

notes.front: An analytics job must read a blob in the archive tier within the hour. What must happen first, and is an hour guaranteed?
notes.back: The blob must be rehydrated to an online tier first, which can take up to 15 hours, so no.
notes.explanation: Reading an archived blob requires rehydrating it to hot, cool or cold first.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Archive access tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To read or download a blob in the archive tier, you must first rehydrate it to an online tier, either hot, cool, or cold. Data in the archive tier can take up to 15 hours to rehydrate, depending on the priority you specify for the rehydration operation.

notes.front: Which operation does Microsoft recommend for most rehydrations from the archive tier?
notes.back: Copy Blob, copying the blob to an online tier.
notes.explanation: Copying can avoid the early deletion penalty if the source blob’s minimum period hasn’t yet passed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Setting or changing a blob’s tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Calling Copy Blob is recommended for most scenarios where you're rehydrating a blob from the archive tier to an online tier, or moving a blob from cool or cold to hot. By copying a blob, you can avoid the early deletion penalty, if the required storage interval for the source blob hasn't yet elapsed.

notes.front: A blob archived only 30 days ago is needed online again, and you want to avoid the archive early deletion penalty. How do you rehydrate it?
notes.back: Copy it to a hot, cool or cold blob with Copy Blob.
notes.explanation: Copying avoids the early deletion penalty, although you then pay capacity for both the source and destination blobs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Setting or changing a blob’s tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By copying a blob, you can avoid the early deletion penalty, if the required storage interval for the source blob hasn't yet elapsed. However, copying a blob results in capacity charges for two blobs, the source blob and the destination blob.

notes.front: Which operation is typically best for moving an existing blob from a warmer tier to a cooler one?
notes.back: Set Blob Tier.
notes.explanation: It can be called directly or through a lifecycle management policy.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Setting or changing a blob’s tier” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By calling the Set Blob Tier operation, either directly or via a lifecycle management policy. Calling Set Blob Tier is typically the best option when you're changing a blob's tier from a warmer tier to a cooler one.

notes.front: What is the default access tier for a new general-purpose v2 storage account, and can it be changed?
notes.back: Hot; you can change it when creating the account or afterwards.
notes.explanation: So unless someone changes it, a new account starts with hot as its default tier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Default account access tier setting” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The default access tier for a new general-purpose v2 storage account is set to the hot tier by default. You can change the default access tier setting when you create a storage account or after it's created.

notes.front: You switch a general-purpose v2 account’s default access tier from hot to cool. Which blobs change tier, and what is charged?
notes.back: Every blob with an inferred tier; you pay write operations for those blobs.
notes.explanation: Blobs with an explicitly set tier keep it, because the default applies only where no tier was set.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Access tiers for blob data”, “Default account access tier setting” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: applies to all blobs in the account for which an access tier hasn't been explicitly set. If you toggle the default access tier setting to a cooler tier in a general-purpose v2 account, then you're charged for write operations (per 10,000) for all blobs for which the access tier is inferred.

notes.front: Blob soft delete keeps deleted objects for a retention period of between {{c1::1 and 365}} days.
notes.explanation: The period covers data that is deleted and data that is overwritten.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How blob soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable blob soft delete for a storage account, you specify a retention period for deleted objects of between 1 and 365 days. The retention period indicates how long the data remains available after it's deleted or overwritten.

notes.front: A policy says deleted blobs must be recoverable for 400 days. Can blob soft delete alone meet it?
notes.back: No. Its retention period can be at most 365 days.
notes.explanation: The retention period for deleted objects must be between 1 and 365 days.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How blob soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable blob soft delete for a storage account, you specify a retention period for deleted objects of between 1 and 365 days.

notes.front: Blob soft delete retention is cut from 30 days to 7. What happens to blobs that were soft-deleted last week?
notes.back: They keep the 30-day retention that applied when they were deleted.
notes.explanation: An updated retention period applies only to data deleted after the change.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How blob soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can change the soft delete retention period at any time. An updated retention period applies only to data that was deleted after the retention period was changed. Any data that was deleted before the retention period was changed is subject to the retention period that was in effect when it was deleted.

notes.front: With blob soft delete on, what does overwriting a blob automatically create?
notes.back: A soft-deleted snapshot of the blob’s state before the write.
notes.explanation: That snapshot is permanently deleted when the retention period expires.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How overwrites are handled when soft delete is enabled” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When blob soft delete is enabled, overwriting a blob automatically creates a soft-deleted snapshot of the blob's state before the write operation. When the retention period expires, the soft-deleted snapshot is permanently deleted.

notes.front: Does blob soft delete protect against deletion of the storage account itself?
notes.back: No. To protect the account, put a lock on the storage account resource.
notes.explanation: Soft delete works on objects inside the account, so the account needs a resource lock instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How blob soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Blob soft delete does not protect against the deletion of a storage account. To protect a storage account from deletion, configure a lock on the storage account resource.

notes.front: Which operation restores a soft-deleted blob, and what else comes back with it?
notes.back: Undelete Blob; it also restores the blob’s soft-deleted snapshots.
notes.explanation: It must be called within the retention period.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “Restoring soft-deleted objects” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can restore soft-deleted blobs or directories (in a hierarchical namespace) by calling the Undelete Blob operation within the retention period. The **Undelete Blob** operation restores a blob and any soft-deleted snapshots associated with it.

notes.front: A user deleted a report blob yesterday. Blob soft delete is on with 14-day retention. Can they read the old report straight away?
notes.back: Not until it is restored with Undelete Blob; then it can be read.
notes.explanation: Data in a soft-deleted blob can’t be read until the object is restored.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “Restoring soft-deleted objects” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't read data in a soft-deleted blob or snapshot until the object is restored.

notes.front: What retention period can container soft delete use, and what is its default?
notes.back: 1 to 365 days; seven days by default.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends at least seven days, and more depending on data volume and how long detection takes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for containers”, “How container soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you enable container soft delete, you can specify a retention period for deleted containers that is between 1 and 365 days. The default retention period is seven days. We recommend a minimum of seven days and increasing the retention period as needed based on data volume and how long it may take to detect and respond to data‑loss events.

notes.front: Which operation recovers a soft-deleted container, and what is restored with it?
notes.back: Restore Container; the container’s blobs, blob versions and snapshots come back too.
notes.explanation: It works only while the retention period is still running.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for containers”, “How container soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: During the retention period, you can recover a deleted container by calling the **Restore Container** operation. When you restore a container, the container's blobs and any blob versions and snapshots are also restored.

notes.front: A container named invoices was deleted, and a colleague has since created a new container called invoices. Can the old one be restored?
notes.back: No. A container must be restored to its original name, and that name is now in use.
notes.explanation: Reusing the original name for a new container blocks restoring the soft-deleted one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for containers”, “How container soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you restore a container, you must restore it to its original name. If the original name is used to create a new container, then you cannot restore the soft-deleted container.

notes.front: A single blob is deleted but its container still exists. Can container soft delete bring the blob back?
notes.back: No. Use blob soft delete or blob versioning instead.
notes.explanation: Container soft delete restores only whole containers and their contents at the time of deletion.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for containers”, “How container soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Container soft delete can restore only whole containers and their contents at the time of deletion. To restore a deleted blob when its parent container hasn't been deleted, you must use blob soft delete or blob versioning.

notes.front: Can blob soft delete on its own restore a deleted container?
notes.back: No. Container soft delete must also be enabled.
notes.explanation: Blob soft delete restores only individual blobs, snapshots, directories or versions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Soft delete for blobs”, “How blob soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use blob soft delete only to restore an individual blob, snapshot, directory (in a hierarchical namespace) or version. To restore a container and its contents, container soft delete must also be enabled for the storage account.

notes.front: What does each new share snapshot save?
notes.back: Only the data that changed since the most recent share snapshot.
notes.explanation: This cuts the time to create the snapshot and the storage cost, since you pay only for changed content.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Share snapshot space usage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Share snapshots are incremental. Only the data that changed after your most recent share snapshot is saved. This feature minimizes the time required to create the share snapshot and saves on storage costs, because you pay only for the changed content.

notes.front: You took share snapshots each day this week and delete all but the newest. Can you still restore the whole share from it?
notes.back: Yes. Only the most recent share snapshot is needed to restore the share.
notes.explanation: Deleting a snapshot removes only the data unique to that snapshot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Share snapshot space usage” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even though share snapshots are saved incrementally, you need to retain only the most recent share snapshot to restore the share. When you delete a share snapshot, only the data unique to that share snapshot is removed.

notes.front: What can you do with a share snapshot once it exists?
notes.back: Read, copy or delete it, but not modify it.
notes.explanation: To move its data to another storage account, you copy it file by file, for example with AzCopy.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Share snapshot capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you create a share snapshot, you can read, copy, or delete it, but you can't modify it. You can't copy a whole share snapshot to another storage account. You have to copy that data file by file, by using AzCopy or other copying mechanisms.

notes.front: How many share snapshots can one Azure file share have, and for how long can they be kept?
notes.back: Up to 200 per share, kept for up to 10 years.
notes.explanation: At 200, older snapshots must be deleted before new ones can be created.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Share snapshot limits” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Files supports up to 200 share snapshots per share. After reaching 200 share snapshots, you must delete older share snapshots to create new ones. You can retain snapshots for up to 10 years.

notes.front: Do share snapshots protect against someone deleting the file share or storage account?
notes.back: No. They give only file-level protection.
notes.explanation: Against those deletions, use soft delete, or lock the storage account or resource group.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Share snapshots provide only file-level protection. They don't prevent accidental deletions on a file share or storage account. To help protect a storage account from accidental deletion, you can either enable soft delete, or lock the storage account and/or the resource group.

notes.front: Tonight a new release of an app that rewrites files on an Azure file share goes live. What cheap safeguard should you take just before it?
notes.back: A share snapshot, so you can return to the earlier data if the release damages it.
notes.explanation: If the new code introduces a bug, you can go back to a previous version of the share’s data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Protect against application error and data corruption” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To help protect against these scenarios, take a share snapshot before you deploy new application code. If a bug or application error is introduced by the new deployment, you can go back to a previous version of your data on that file share.

notes.front: How do you restore an earlier version of a file from a share snapshot?
notes.back: Copy the file from the snapshot to its base share or another location; the snapshot isn’t promoted.
notes.explanation: Even a whole share is restored by copying file by file from the snapshot.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Copying data back to a share from share snapshot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can copy individual files in a file share snapshot over to its base share or any other location. You can restore an earlier version of a file or restore the complete file share by copying file by file from the share snapshot. The share snapshot isn't promoted to base share.

notes.front: A Windows user needs yesterday’s copy of one spreadsheet from a Server Message Block file share that has daily snapshots. Where can they find it?
notes.back: On the Previous Versions tab in Windows File Explorer, then copy it out.
notes.explanation: From that snapshot view, files can be copied to a local path with ordinary file operations or Robocopy.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use share snapshots with Azure Files”, “Copying data back to a local drive from share snapshot” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On Windows, you can access SMB file share snapshots from the **Previous Versions** tab in Windows File Explorer. When you access a snapshot view by using this method, you can copy files and folders to a local path by using standard file operations or Robocopy.

notes.front: By default, soft-deleted file shares are kept for {{c1::7}} days.
notes.explanation: Any period from 1 to 365 days can be set, counted from when the share is deleted.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, the retention period for file shares is 7 days, but you can specify any retention period between 1 and 365 days. The retention period clock starts when the file share is deleted.

notes.front: Policy says a deleted file share must be recoverable for 30 days. What do you configure?
notes.back: Soft delete for file shares on the storage account, with a 30-day retention period.
notes.explanation: The default is 7 days, but any period from 1 to 365 days can be set.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, the retention period for file shares is 7 days, but you can specify any retention period between 1 and 365 days.

notes.front: At what level is soft delete for file shares switched on, and is it on for new accounts?
notes.back: At the storage account level, for all its file shares; new accounts have it on by default.
notes.explanation: You can still enable or disable it on new or existing accounts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Soft delete for file shares is enabled at the storage account level so the soft delete settings apply to all file shares within a storage account. New storage accounts have soft delete enabled by default, but you can enable or disable soft delete as desired for new or existing storage accounts.

notes.front: You want soft delete on for share A but off for share B, both in the same storage account. Can you?
notes.back: No. The setting applies to all file shares in the storage account.
notes.explanation: It is enabled at the storage account level rather than per share.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Soft delete for file shares is enabled at the storage account level so the soft delete settings apply to all file shares within a storage account.

notes.front: What does soft delete for file shares restore, compared with share snapshots?
notes.back: Soft delete restores whole deleted shares; share snapshots or backup restore individual deleted files.
notes.explanation: Soft delete works only at the file share level.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Soft delete works only at the file share level. If you want to restore deleted files, you can use share snapshots or Azure file share backup.

notes.front: How do you permanently delete a soft-deleted file share before its retention period ends?
notes.back: Undelete the share, disable soft delete, then delete the share again.
notes.explanation: Afterwards, remember to re-enable soft delete to protect the account’s other shares.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “How soft delete works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To permanently delete a file share in a soft delete state before its expiry time, you must undelete the share, disable soft delete, and then delete the share again. If desired, remember to reenable soft delete for the storage account to protect other file shares from accidental deletion.

notes.front: In the portal, how do you find a soft-deleted file share so you can undelete it?
notes.back: Turn on Show deleted shares on the file share blade, then select the share and undelete.
notes.explanation: Soft-deleted shares are listed in a Deleted state only when that option is on.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure file share soft delete”, “Restore soft deleted file share” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On the file share blade, enable **Show deleted shares** to display any shares that are soft deleted. This displays any shares currently in a **Deleted** state.

notes.front: On which blob properties can a lifecycle rule’s conditions be based?
notes.back: Creation time, last modified time, and last accessed time.
notes.explanation: Last accessed time can be used only if access time tracking is enabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Lifecycle management policy features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Conditions are based on the following three blob properties: Creation Time, Last Modified Time, and Last Accessed Time (if access time tracking is enabled)

notes.front: Can a lifecycle rule’s filter exclude certain blobs?
notes.back: No. Filters can only specify which blobs to include.
notes.explanation: When a rule has several filters, they are combined with a logical AND.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Lifecycle management policy features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If more than one filter is defined, a logical AND runs on all filters. You can use a filter to specify which blobs to include. A filter provides no means to specify which blobs to exclude.

notes.front: You want a lifecycle rule that deletes every blob in a container except those under the prefix keep/. Can a filter express “except”?
notes.back: No. Filters only include blobs, so target the blobs to delete by their own prefixes or tags.
notes.explanation: A filter provides no means to exclude blobs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Lifecycle management policy features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use a filter to specify which blobs to include. A filter provides no means to specify which blobs to exclude.

notes.front: After you add or edit lifecycle policy rules, it can take up to {{c1::24 hours}} for the changes to take effect.
notes.explanation: The first run of the policy may also not start until then.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Policy execution” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you add or edit the rules of a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours for changes to go into effect and for the first execution to start.

notes.front: An hour ago you added a lifecycle rule to delete old logs, but nothing has been deleted yet. What is the likely explanation?
notes.back: The rule may not have taken effect yet: changes can take up to 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Both the change and the first run can take up to a day to start.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Policy execution” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you add or edit the rules of a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours for changes to go into effect and for the first execution to start.

notes.front: What is the recommended way to remove a lifecycle policy?
notes.back: Disable it first, wait 24 hours, then delete it.
notes.explanation: A run already in progress stops within 24 hours of the policy being disabled.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Policy execution” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you disable all of the rules in a policy, then the policy becomes inactive. If a run is already in progress, that run comes to a stop within 24 hours, and no new runs are scheduled. It's recommended to disable a policy first, wait 24 hours and then delete policy.

notes.front: Can a lifecycle policy move blobs between tiers in a premium block blob account?
notes.back: No. Tiering isn’t yet supported there.
notes.explanation: In other accounts, tiering applies only to block blobs, not append or page blobs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Known issues and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Tiering isn't yet supported in a premium block blob storage account. For all other accounts, tiering is allowed only on block blobs and not for append and page blobs.

notes.front: Can a lifecycle management policy rehydrate archived blobs to an online tier?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: It is one of the known limitations of lifecycle management, so rehydration must be done another way.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview”, “Known issues and limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Lifecycle management policies can't be used to rehydrate blobs to an online tier.

notes.front: Blobs are busy for a month, then rarely read. You want them moved to a cooler tier automatically and deleted after a year. Which feature does this?
notes.back: A blob lifecycle management policy.
notes.choices:
A) Object replication
B) A blob lifecycle management policy
C) Blob versioning
D) Container soft delete
notes.choicesExplained: A copies blobs to another account. C keeps earlier versions of blobs. D recovers deleted containers. None of them tiers or expires data on a schedule.
notes.explanation: Lifecycle rules move objects to cooler tiers when unused and delete them at the end of their lifecycle.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Transition current versions of a blob, previous versions of a blob, or blob snapshots to a cooler storage tier if these objects aren't accessed or modified for a period of time, to optimize for cost.

notes.front: With blob versioning enabled, {{c1::every write operation}} to a blob creates a new version.
notes.explanation: This is why versioning might add costs, and a lifecycle policy can delete old versions automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you enable blob versioning for a storage account, every write operation to a blob in that account results in the creation of a new version. For this reason, enabling blob versioning might result in extra costs. To minimize costs, use a lifecycle management policy to automatically delete old versions.

notes.front: After blob versioning is switched on, storage costs climb for an app that rewrites the same large blob every few minutes. Why, and what limits it?
notes.back: Each write creates a new version; a lifecycle management policy can delete old versions automatically.
notes.explanation: Every write creates a version, so frequent rewrites pile up versions that you pay to store.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you enable blob versioning for a storage account, every write operation to a blob in that account results in the creation of a new version. For this reason, enabling blob versioning might result in extra costs. To minimize costs, use a lifecycle management policy to automatically delete old versions.

notes.front: When you modify a blob that has versioning on, what happens to its current version?
notes.back: It becomes a previous version, and a new current version captures the update.
notes.explanation: A blob has only one current version at a time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “How blob versioning works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A blob can have only one current version at a time. When you create a new blob, a single version exists, and that version is the current version. When you modify an existing blob, the current version becomes a previous version. A new version is created to capture the updated state, and that new version is the current version.

notes.front: Can blob versioning recover a storage account or container that was deleted by accident?
notes.back: No, neither. To prevent the storage account being deleted, lock the storage account resource.
notes.explanation: Versioning protects blobs, not the account or container that holds them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “How blob versioning works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Blob versioning can't help you recover from the accidental deletion of a storage account or container. To prevent accidental deletion of the storage account, configure a lock on the storage account resource.

notes.front: Users sometimes overwrite blobs with bad data and need to roll back to any earlier state of that blob. Which feature fits best?
notes.back: Blob versioning.
notes.choices:
A) Blob versioning
B) Container soft delete
C) Soft delete for file shares
D) A blob lifecycle management policy
notes.choicesExplained: B restores deleted containers, not earlier states of a blob. C applies to Azure file shares. D moves or deletes blobs; it doesn’t keep earlier states.
notes.explanation: Versioning keeps earlier versions of each blob, which can be used to recover data after it is modified or deleted.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can enable Blob storage versioning to automatically maintain previous versions of an object. When you enable blob versioning, you can access earlier versions of a blob to recover your data if it's modified or deleted.

notes.front: What happens to existing versions when you disable blob versioning?
notes.back: They remain accessible, and no new versions are created.
notes.explanation: Disabling versioning doesn’t delete any existing blobs, versions or snapshots.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “Enable or disable blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Disabling blob versioning doesn't delete existing blobs, versions, or snapshots. When you turn off blob versioning, any existing versions remain accessible in your storage account. No new versions are subsequently created.

notes.front: After blob versioning is disabled, what happens when you update a blob?
notes.back: The update overwrites its data without saving the previous state; existing versions persist.
notes.explanation: Modifying the current version now creates a blob that isn’t a version.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “Enable or disable blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After versioning is disabled, modifying the current version creates a blob that isn't a version. All subsequent updates to the blob overwrite its data without saving the previous state. All existing versions persist as previous versions.

notes.front: You try to disable blob versioning on an account, but the account takes part in object replication. What must you do first?
notes.back: Delete the account’s object replication policies.
notes.explanation: Object replication relies on blob versioning, so versioning can’t be turned off while its policies exist.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “Enable or disable blob versioning” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Object replication relies on blob versioning. Before you can disable blob versioning, you must delete any object replication policies on the account.

notes.front: How do blob versions differ from blob snapshots in the way they are created?
notes.back: Snapshots are created manually; versions are created automatically on each write or delete once versioning is on.
notes.explanation: Both are read-only, point-in-time copies of a blob.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “Blob versioning and blob snapshots” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A blob snapshot is a read-only copy of a blob taken at a specific point in time. Blob snapshots and blob versions are similar, but you or your application manually create a snapshot, while a blob version is created automatically during a write or delete operation when you enable blob versioning for your storage account.

notes.front: With versioning and blob soft delete both on, can Undelete Blob restore just one soft-deleted version?
notes.back: No, and no restored version becomes the current version.
notes.explanation: To get a current version back, you copy a previous version over it with Copy Blob.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Blob versioning”, “Restoring a soft-deleted version” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can't restore only a single soft-deleted version. Restoring soft-deleted versions by using the **Undelete Blob** operation doesn't promote any version to be the current version. To restore the current version, first restore all soft-deleted versions, and then use the Copy Blob operation to copy a previous version to a new current version.
